Wuthering Heights

Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights is a film that wants very badly to shock you. Whether it wants to move you is another question entirely.

🚨 WOKE TRAP WARNING

This film draws you in for a significant portion of its runtime with traditional or neutral content before springing its woke agenda. Know before you go!

The literary pedigree acts as bait for audiences who wouldn't normally sit through what is essentially '50 Shades of Bronte.' The film doesn't hide its sexual content for long, but the prestige packaging and classic novel branding draw in traditional audiences before the provocations begin.

Overall Perspective

Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights is a film that wants very badly to shock you. Whether it wants to move you is another question entirely.

On paper, this should be a conservative viewer's dream. A prestige adaptation of one of the great works of English literature, shot on gorgeous 35mm film in the actual Yorkshire Dales, starring two of Hollywood's most bankable leads. And there are moments, real ones, where the film touches something genuine. The moors are breathtaking. Linus Sandgren's cinematography captures the wild beauty of Bronte country with a tactile warmth that digital cameras simply cannot replicate.

But Fennell is not interested in faithfulness. She is interested in sensation. The film opens with a nun watching a public hanging. The condemned man gets an erection as he dies. This is Fennell planting her flag. If you are hoping for a respectful treatment of Bronte's text, leave now.

The BDSM subplot between servants Joseph and Zillah has no basis in the novel. The transformation of Heathcliff's abuse of Isabella into a consensual kink arrangement is more troubling. In Bronte's novel, Heathcliff's treatment of Isabella is unambiguously cruel. Fennell rewrites this as a mutually understood BDSM relationship. This is a deeply modern, sex-positive reframing of what Bronte intended as a portrait of evil. The scene where Catherine masturbates on the moors is pure Fennell provocation with no textual basis whatsoever.

The casting of Hong Chau as Nelly Dean is the film's most obvious ideological signal. Fennell reimagines her as a lord's illegitimate daughter, which functions as a backstory justification for casting a Vietnamese-American actress in a role that is specifically English. The film never addresses Nelly's appearance within its own world.

What complicates the picture is the Heathcliff casting controversy, which came from the progressive side. Many scholars interpret him as a person of color based on Bronte's text. Fennell cast white Australian Jacob Elordi and faced significant backlash from progressives wanting a non-white Heathcliff.

Where the film genuinely connects with traditional values is in the raw emotional power of the Catherine-Heathcliff relationship. The central love story operates on an almost primal level. This is a tale about two people who are soul-bonded in a way that transcends social convention, class, marriage, and even death. The film's final image of Heathcliff cradling Catherine's dead body carries real weight.

The period setting immerses viewers in a world of English manor houses, wild moorland, and the kind of landscapes that form the bedrock of British cultural identity. Martin Clunes brings rough authenticity to Mr. Earnshaw. The Yorkshire Dales locations are stunning.

But these traditional strengths keep getting undercut by Fennell's compulsive need to shock. She cannot leave a scene alone. Every tender moment gets an edge of transgression pushed into it. The result is a film that is technically accomplished, occasionally moving, and fundamentally unserious about its source material. Fennell treats Wuthering Heights less as a story to be told and more as a canvas for her own fixations.

Conservative viewers should know that this is not the Wuthering Heights of the 1939 Olivier film or even the 1992 Fiennes version. It is Emerald Fennell's psychosexual fever dream loosely draped over Bronte's plot. The traditional bones of the story survive, barely, beneath the provocation.

Woke Trap Warning

Trap Present: Yes — Degree: partial. This film wraps itself in the prestige of Emily Bronte's classic novel and lures traditional audiences with the promise of a sweeping period romance. What it actually delivers is Emerald Fennell's trademark shock-value provocation: gratuitous BDSM sequences, a public hanging with a visible erection in the opening shot, masturbation on the moors, and a fundamental rewrite of the source material that transforms Isabella Linton's abuse into consensual kink. The race-swap of Nelly Dean is never explained within the story. Conservative viewers expecting a faithful Bronte adaptation will find something quite different.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Emerald Fennell

MODERATELY WOKE

British filmmaker whose work consistently centers female sexuality, power dynamics, and the subversion of traditional narratives. Won the Oscar for Best Original Screenplay for Promising Young Woman. Her entire filmography explores feminist provocation and psychosexual transgression.

Writer: Emerald Fennell

Sole credited screenwriter (based on Bronte's novel). As with her previous films, Fennell writes and directs, meaning the creative vision is undiluted. Her screenplay adds significant sexual content not present in Bronte's text and reframes key moral dynamics through a modern, sex-positive lens.

Producers

  • Margot Robbie & Josey McNamara (LuckyChap Entertainment) — Robbie's production company consistently produces female-led and female-directed films. Progressive-leaning but commercially savvy.
  • Emerald Fennell — See director profile. As co-producer on her own film, her creative control is near-total.
  • MRC (Media Rights Capital) — Major financing entity. Follows talent and commercial viability. No consistent ideological signal.

Fidelity Casting Analysis MODIFIED

One major race-swap (Nelly Dean); Heathcliff's canonical racial ambiguity erased by casting a white actor.

The casting makes two notable departures from source fidelity, pulling in opposite directions. Nelly Dean, a Yorkshire servant in Bronte's novel, is played by Vietnamese-American actress Hong Chau and rewritten as a lord's illegitimate daughter. Heathcliff, described by Bronte as dark-skinned and resembling a Lascar, is played by white Australian Jacob Elordi. Edgar Linton is played by British-Pakistani actor Shazad Latif. The supporting cast is largely faithful to the source material's demographics.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adult viewers should approach this film with clear eyes. It is not the Wuthering Heights you grew up with. It is Emerald Fennell's personal interpretation, heavy on sexual provocation and light on fidelity to Bronte's moral framework. The R rating is well earned. That said, the film accidentally proves a conservative point. All of Fennell's provocations land as noise. What actually moves the audience is the oldest story in the book: two people who love each other so deeply that nothing in the world can contain it. The traditional core of Bronte's novel is so powerful that even Fennell cannot smother it. The whitewashing controversy reveals the circular logic of identity-politics casting. Progressives demanded a non-white Heathcliff but had no complaint about the race-swapped Nelly Dean and Edgar Linton. The rules of diversity casting only flow in one direction.

Parental Guidance

This film is rated R and the rating is fully justified. Parents should exercise extreme caution. Sexual content is severe: the film opens with a public hanging featuring a visible erection, includes multiple explicit sexual encounters, BDSM relationships with degradation and power play, and a masturbation scene outdoors. Violence is moderate with a severe whipping, public execution, and disturbing death scenes. Catherine's death from sepsis following a miscarriage is depicted with graphic detail. Not appropriate for viewers under 17. The sexual content is explicit and pervasive enough that even mature teenagers may find it uncomfortable, particularly the BDSM elements and the film's non-judgmental framing of behaviors the source material condemns.
